I have much love for the American people, but I support the actions of our government.

children.textRawHtml:
As a fellow Canadian. Our neighbor is the world's biggest economy. Despite their current "challenges" they are still very close to us in values and culture. Our paths are interlocked. We are not going to decouple from the USA and it's not in our interest to do so.

When a Canadian new grad is faced with an option of going to work in SV or in China which do they prefer? Between Chinese values and American values which do we prefer? A society with no freedom of speech? Where people are arbitrarily jailed if they voice an opinion against the government? Where the government places citizens in concentration and re-education camps and runs them over with tanks? I mean to me the choice is clear.

How many large American companies have offices in Canada? How many people and what slice of the economy does this support? Lots.

So yes, the US has drifted and is drifting from the ideal. And maybe it was never the ideal. But it's much closer to us than China in every imaginable facet and will likely remain so for the next many decades. We need to filter the noise out, definitely stand firmly for what we believe in, but also compromise and look at the longer term.

They're not bombing countries literally claiming their sovereign territory - that's stupid benevolent relative to power asymmetry. PRC inherited all territorial disputes and resolved ~12/14 land border disputes, most with more concessions. In SCS, which is multi party, they're the only ones who made any concession (11 dash to 9 dash), and offered resource sharing in lieu intractable resolution. Meaning PRC not only did not create any border disputes, but proactively resolved most peacefully and tries to resolve current peacefully. There's a reason most remaining disputes are from democracies where ceding or even splitting is political suicide. And frankly party in territorial disputes who thinks they should get 100 vs PRC should get 0 (basically what losers in wars gets) is retarded and in the wrong... and frankly that is the level of delulu PRC is peacefully dealing with.

That makes PRC like most benevolent rising power in recorded history. There's no fallacy, one measure powers behavior relative to other comparable powers - and relative to all historic powers - PRC is objectively benevolent.

comments.author: milkytron
comments.textRawHtml:
The part that still bothers me so much about the US vs Swartz case is that JSTOR didn't pursue civil litigation against Aaron. It was the US government that pursued him.

There was little for the government to lose in the case. In a case vs Meta, at the scale it has reached, it could have wide ranging economic implications limiting the investment in AI, which the US is absolutely not willing to pursue at this point in time (or possibly ever).

Basically, being a rich public company provides legal advantages when the US government has similar goals.

The whole thing is incredibly sad and exposes the hypocrisy of the US court system and government as a whole.

RIP Aaron.
comments.textZhHtml:
US vs Swartz 案中最让我困扰的是 JSTOR 没有对 Aaron 提起民事诉讼。追捕他的是美国政府。

政府在此案中几乎没有什么损失。在针对 Meta 的案件中，就其规模而言，它可能会产生广泛的经济影响，限制对人工智能的投资，而美国目前（或可能永远）绝对不愿意追求人工智能。

基本上，当美国政府有类似的目标时，成为一家富有的上市公司会提供法律优势。

整件事令人难以置信的悲伤，暴露了美国法院系统和整个政府的虚伪。

安息吧。亚伦。

Maybe the real issue is selective outrage about legal injustice. I totally agree that this was wrong and he should not have been prosecuted but a large part of the effort that dealt this injustice to him was facilitated by the fact that the vast majority of people willfully turn a blind eye when the same thing or worse happens to people are not of their ilk. If we were to finally stand up and say that justice for all means justice for ALL; we might be able to prevent the next Aaron Swartz.

Edit: As someone that has done both state and fed time, the thing that makes me the saddest here is that the charges would have been drastically reduced if not dismissed and his appeals would have had a high probability of success. They use this "scare tatic" so much and I understand why it works; the possibility of facing those years is terrifying. I don't mean that in any demeaning manner, 25/26 and never having done time I cannot imagine how terrified he must have been.

Edit: I would also like to bring attention to the fact that M. Zuckerberg aggressively pursues these types of cases against people for doing far less than he has done.

children.author: AnthonyMouse
children.textRawHtml:
> If it applied equally to everyone, then more people would be outraged as it affected them.

In order to do this you need to have laws that are designed to be reasonable for people to actually follow instead of laws that are designed to allow prosecutors to find a violation whenever they want to.

Actually enforcing them would create pressure to do that, but it would also create pressure to go back to selective enforcement when powerful people object to being subjected to the unreasonableness of existing laws.

A better solution might be to make a showing of selective enforcement a means to strike down a law. If you can show that someone else was doing the same thing without being charged then the prosecution either has to charge them too or that law is struck down and no one can be charged with it anymore.

Then instead of the incentive not to charge powerful people creating pressure for selective enforcement, the same incentive creates pressure to strike down the laws that can't reasonably be uniformly enforced.

为了做到这一点，你需要制定合理的法律，让人们真正遵守，而不是旨在允许检察官随时发现违规行为的法律。

实际上执行这些法律会产生这样做的压力，但当有权势的人反对受到约束时，也会产生返回选择性执法的压力。现有法律的不合理性。

更好的解决方案可能是将选择性执法的表现作为废除法律的手段。如果你能证明其他人在没有受到指控的情况下做了同样的事情，那么检方要么必须对他们也提出指控，要么法律被废除，没有人可以再被指控。

然后，不是激励不起诉有权势的人，为选择性执法创造压力，同样的激励会产生压力，废除那些无法合理统一执行的法律。

I know that's a skill that I have, and I used it so many times it became effortless, but it all goes to one of jokes I like - that asks how do you eat an elephant. Easy - with a fork.

So in that particular case I have a keyboard and it's misbehaving. I know that by some dark magic I can make it behave as I want and that software on Windows can do that.

So I think, "ok, how does it communicate?" - with Bluetooth, obviously. So my next thought it: can I transmit over bluetooth magic bytes that do exactly like this. I definitely have a device on my computer, so I can try to make it.

From that it's all about "how to send arbitrary stuff from bluetooth" search. Instinct tells me there has to be a library, or that at least on person on world wide web tried to do something similar.

If I find even single instance of this, I'm home - read what they did, try to figure out if I can adjust it and do so. Hocus pocus - binary switcher happens.

Though, in the end, it's all about approach. I found many people say "I don't know how to do it, so I don't". My approach is "I rarely know what do, but that doesn't stop me from trying". And this trying new stuff brings practice for the next unknown endeavor.
children.textZhHtml:
我知道这是我拥有的一项技能，而且我使用了很多次，它变得毫不费力，但这一切都源于我喜欢的一个笑话 - 那问你如何吃掉大象。简单 - 用叉子。

所以在这种特殊情况下，我有一个键盘，但它表现不佳。我知道通过某种黑魔法我可以让它按照我想要的方式运行，Windows 上的软件也可以做到这一点。

所以我想，“好吧，它是如何通信的？” - 显然是通过蓝牙。所以我的下一个想法是：我可以通过蓝牙魔法字节进行传输吗？我的计算机上肯定有一个设备，所以我可以尝试制作它。

从这一切都是关于“如何从蓝牙发送任意内容”搜索。直觉告诉我必须有一个图书馆，或者至少在万维网上有人试图做类似的事情。

如果我发现哪怕是一个这样的例子，我就回家了 - 阅读他们做了什么，尝试弄清楚我是否可以调整它并这样做。 Hocus pocus - 二进制切换器发生了。

不过，最终，这都是关于方法的。我发现很多人说“我不知道该怎么做，所以我不做”。我的方法是“我很少知道该做什么，但这并不妨碍我尝试”。这种尝试新事物为下一个未知的尝试带来了练习。

Copyright law desperately needs a production requirement or allowance.

The copyright owner must make new copies of the work available; the price must be no greater than the original price (not inflation adjusted). And if they fail to do so, anyone may produce copies and escrow the original price (less the cost of production) for collection by the copyright holder.

That means that orphan works are effectively in the public domain. Calculus professors can ask students to get the cheaper 2nd edition, not the latest 22nd edition. And a company like Google could make scanned works available in their entirety for a small amount of money for each work. And the copyright holder still gets their end, without having to arrange a printing or hold stock.

children.author: ndiddy
children.textRawHtml:
"Controlled digital lending" is not a generic term for "lending digital items". It specifically refers to the practice of a library digitizing physical materials in its collection, then lending them digitally based on a 1:1 owned-to-loaned ratio. The idea is that the library should be able to treat digitized versions of a book the same way it treats the physical book, and the total number of physical and digital copies of the book that are lent out at once should never be more than the number of physical copies that the library has.

In contrast to this, the e-book lending practiced by most libraries with publisher blessing involves the library purchasing special library-specific e-book licenses from the publisher. These licenses contain various contractual restrictions, such as the library having to re-purchase the e-book after a certain amount of time or after a certain number of borrows.
children.textZhHtml:
“受控数字借贷”不是“借贷数字物品”的通用术语。它特指图书馆将其馆藏中的实物资料数字化，然后按照1:1的自借比以数字方式出借的做法。这个想法是，图书馆应该能够像对待实体书一样对待书籍的数字化版本，并且一次借出的实体书和数字书的总数永远不应超过图书馆拥有的实体书的数量。

与此相反，大多数在出版商支持下的图书馆实行的电子书借阅涉及图书馆从出版商那里购买特定于图书馆的电子书许可证。这些许可证包含各种合同限制，例如图书馆必须在一定时间或借阅一定次数后重新购买电子书。

comments.author: afc
comments.textRawHtml:
> Both incidents were capacity failures at their core. We failed to scale critical components before demand exceeded their capacity.

This is the wrong way to think about this because there's no such thing as infinite capacity. A large distributed system will be simultaneously mostly idle and (in some subcomponents) overloaded. The root cause is not "a component didn't have enough capacity (because of auto scaling failures)", but rather "this complex system collapses (rather than degrade gracefully) when demand exceeds capacity".

When components reach capacity limits, the excess traffic of the lowest priority should be rejected. Rejected traffic should not be retried — in fact, not only should clients not retry these errors, these errors should cause client-side throttling. Traffic isolation should be applied — if the cause of the overload is a single client/customer system, no other system should be affected.

Nearly a decade ago I wrote about some of the techniques we applied at Google to implement these protections: https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/ Most other large internet services have since copied them, afaik.
comments.textZhHtml:
> 这两起事件的核心都是容量故障。我们未能在需求超出其容量之前扩展关键组件。

这是错误的思考方式，因为不存在无限容量这样的事情。大型分布式系统将同时大部分处于空闲状态和（在某些子组件中）过载。根本原因不是“某个组件没有足够的容量（因为自动伸缩失败）”，而是“当需求超过容量时，这个复杂的系统就会崩溃（而不是优雅地降级）”。

当组件达到容量限制时，最低优先级的多余流量应该被拒绝。被拒绝的流量不应该重试——事实上，客户端不仅不应该重试这些错误，这些错误还应该导致客户端限制。应应用流量隔离 - 如果过载的原因是单个客户端/客户系统，则不应影响其他系统。

大约十年前，我写了一篇有关我们在 Google 为实现这些保护而应用的一些技术的文章：https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/据我所知，大多数其他大型互联网服务都已复制它们。

children.author: solatic

> you want to move these decisions into the application tier as much as possible

I actually agree, but this is a luxury that most large companies cannot politically prioritize (it is not Product/Sales-driven, see earlier comment). Especially when the company is large, and there are dozens if not hundreds of developer teams in a polyglot microservice environment, pushing application-level handling of these concerns is virtually impossible without executive support, and because it doesn't move the bottom line in an easily measurable way, you won't get executive support.

Companies much prefer infrastructure-based solutions to these problems, even if they're coarser, because the relatively small number of people who need to be involved makes it politically feasible. Easy example off the top of my head - mutual TLS encrypting east-west traffic has been implementable at the application layer for decades, but it was a pipe dream until service meshes made it easy to deploy (it's still a pipe dream for many orgs that refuse to schedule any infra work not Product/Sales-driven though).

comments.author: ehnto
comments.textRawHtml:
One of the biggest causes of slowness is just waiting for web requests. The fact that so much software is either online or built using the same stack even if it isn't, puts all that software in this blocked/waiting state constantly while using it.

Anyone not in the US feels this even more since so much online is US hosted, 300ms for every little interaction adds up quick.

If your software has the affordance of a waiting dialogue or loading wheel for many of its UI controls, you are building with this default blocked assumption. Even if you are building something web based, ask yourself if that's actually necessary for your software or if you could build it differently to avoid constant UI blocking.

children.author: 59nadir
children.textRawHtml:
This is an incomplete and quite superficial view of what is going on out there, in my opinion. I've worked on plenty of projects where the assumption was that since the round-trip to the server is going to take almost 100ms that'll dwarf anything that's going to happen on the server itself, justifying poor choices that lead to potentially adding a whopping 100ms onto that number. These numbers only get larger with a larger perceived "Nothing we can do about it" budget as well, programmers often feel justified in doing just about anything once round-trip time grows, not understanding that they're just adding to an already existing problem.

On top of that: Creating software that isn't outright wasteful in terms of performance isn't even hard, it's just a matter of not doing ridiculously dumb things. The problem I've observed in teams I've worked with is that the majority of programmers don't even know what the dumb things are, and wouldn't know how to even approach making something that's halfway fast.

Edit:

Unfortunately I think posts like these are only going to make the problem worse, because now people are going to ask for voodoo solutions to performance issues, when the answer to their problems was usually just "Maybe stop creating wasteful intermediate structures and just walk an array like a sane person" in 99% of cases. The first leg of any optimization journey in the average programmer's code will likely net tens or hundreds of times faster code, and that's actually all people were asking for.

The knowledge required to make those changes and understand them is fairly minimal, but the kinds of people who have to create spinners for webmail interfaces, have their application add 150ms on top of whatever round-trip you have for processing things counted in 5 digits, etc., have never bothered to even learn those things.

comments.author: openasocket
comments.textRawHtml:
For those that don't know, grand juries declining an indictment is extremely rare. A grand jury is basically a check on prosecution, that they have to have some initial evidence before charging someone with a felony. The standards are much lower than the subsequent criminal proceedings.

The grand jury only hears from the prosecution, there is no defense involved. Only a majority of the grand jury has to sign off, not unanimous like in an actual trial. The standard of evidence is just probable cause, not beyond a reasonable doubt. The rules of evidence are relaxed, meaning hearsay and other evidence can potentially be introduced that would normally be barred from a trial.

Because of the above, the rate of indictment from a grand jury is very high, over 90%. Most prosecutors will go their entire careers without getting a "no true bill" (meaning the grand jury did not sign off on an indictment). There's a saying that "a grand jury would indict a ham sandwich." So the fact that there was no indictment here is a big deal. It will probably hurt that prosecutor's career.

comments.author: hibikir
comments.textRawHtml:
The anecdote about the garden of earthly delights is going to be relatable even for art students. I've met art teachers that ended up "trapped" in Madrid by the Prado Museum: A green, American future Ph.D student that was heading to Greece to specialize in old greek art. But instead of flying straight there, they stopped at Madrid to see the Prado, and were never able to leave. Changed their direction immediately, and ended up teaching in Madrid, and retiring there, because one of the countless masterpieces in there stole their life plans away.

There's more famous museums, and it doesn't have the most popular paintings for non specialist, but it's just haymaker after haymaker, in every single room. And that's leaving the modern art to the Reina Sofia, a short walk away. (Although I guess keeping late Goya there is kind of cheating, as I'd argue he becomes a pioneer of modern art after the war starts)

Books might require quite a bit of work before you can tell they are eternal masterpieces. Seeing the depths of some forms of music might involve not-so-impressive efforts earlier, just to get to the good parts. The very best paintings in the world, in person, can stop people cold. Large format efforts that demand attention even when you don't consider every single small decision.

The Garden of Earthly Delights used to be stuck in a corner, at the edge of one of the wings of the Prado. As if "oh well, I guess it fits here, near all the medieval art". It counted as an ambush.

children.author: encomiast
children.textRawHtml:
Possibly the best thing about Washington D.C. is that the National Gallery of Art (along with, I think, all the Smithsonian) is free. This means you just take a casual stroll through without any of the pressure of having spent a sizable sum like you might to visit a place like the Art Institute in Chicago. In Chicago a visit is an event, you need to see the Seurat, the Grant Wood, etc. You've spent money and you need make it count.

In D.C. you can literally walk in, go look at the big Joan Mitchell for 10 minutes and continue on your day. Or you can wander through a room you've never been interested in and find something and then go to lunch. Without the commitment to get everything done, you are suddenly free.

Good libraries (edit: even mediocre libraries) also have this quality.

children.author: bluGill
children.textRawHtml:
Many museums have a membership. For one price you can visit the museum any time you want. I strongly recommend everyone do this for all their local museums. It changes the experience when you don't feel bad about wasting the admission because you only have an hour. Particularly small local museums where spending all day isn't worth it, but if you have to pay admission you feel compelled to spend all day to get your money's worth.

Some of them also include reduced price admission to others of the same time. My local zoo isn't very big, but the membership means half price admission to a very good zoo just a couple hours away. My local science museum got me free admission to many other science museums and children's museums. My local historic farm got me into a lot of interesting historical sites. Be sure to understand what you get and take advantage of it on vacations.

I strongly recommend you get the version that lets you bring two guests. When my parents or some other friend from out of town comes to visit we have something interesting to show them (and if they are not having fun we can leave early).

comments.author: dajonker
comments.textRawHtml:
Popover, dialog, invoker commands, our entire production app uses these everywhere and it works really well! The fact that dialogs and popovers are rendered on the "top layer" and that nested popovers are also automatically stacked on top of each other and have 'cascading close' shows how well these standards were designed.

The only hard thing is still to position a popover near the element that triggers it, such as when you want to create a context menu that has to render above/below the button that triggered it. There is anchor positioning in CSS now but support is still limited and I find it hard to wrap my head around.

LLMs are also terrible at these new standards. If they even know about them, they often think they're not baseline yet and they have almost zero training data compared to the giant mountain of weird JS and CSS that people had to use before the introduction of these standards.

children.author: doginasuit
children.textRawHtml:
> The only hard thing is still to position a popover near the element that triggers it, such as when you want to create a context menu that has to render above/below the button that triggered it.

If you put something like this in your popover class, it will resolve to the button that called it when position-anchor is not set:

top: anchor(bottom);

I'm not sure how widely supported it is but I've been using it in Firefox/Chrome.
children.textZhHtml:
> 唯一困难的事情仍然是将弹出框放置在触发它的元素附近，例如当您想要创建一个必须在触发它的按钮上方/下方呈现的上下文菜单时。

如果您在弹出框类中放置类似的内容，它将解析为在未设置位置锚点时调用它的按钮：

top:anchor(bottom);

我不确定支持的范围有多大是的，但我一直在 Firefox/Chrome 中使用它。

children.author: extra88
children.textRawHtml: All current browsers support anchor positioning including popover buttons being the implicit anchor. However, the anchor positioning polyfill does not support this, it requires an explicit anchor-name.
children.textZhHtml: 所有当前浏览器都支持锚点定位，包括作为隐式锚点的弹出按钮。然而，锚点定位polyfill不支持这一点，它需要一个显式的锚点名称。

children.author: dajonker
children.textRawHtml:
It's a small team of four, everyone works on the "full stack" which is Rails with HTMX and very little JS. As the lead dev, I am usually the one to make the decision that we should use the modern browser standards.

It's a niche B2B SaaS app and luckily we know most of our users personally. They all use modern browsers, usually Chrome or Edge on Windows. There is not a lot of mobile usage although we do support it.
